brief: Morgan Stanley reaffirms its call that the US faces a 57 GW gross data center power shortfall through 2028, or 32 GW net of time-to-power solutions (34% of demand), after revising US compute share to 55% from 60% but raising non-AI demand, leaving the net figure unchanged. Nvidia and Broadcom commentary confirms power, not chips, is now the binding constraint, but the firm stays convicted both can hit their combined ~$800bn 12-month AI revenue outlook and 2027 numbers, given management's visibility into chip placement and geographic diversification. Risk is downstream: ASICs could lose share to GPUs given lower tokens-per-watt, and a demand pause would hit memory, optics, and power/analog components hardest. Power access is concentrating among credit-worthy hyperscalers (60-95% of global capacity adds), with Amazon well-positioned and Google more exposed given its '27/'28 build pace. International expansion (Australia, Asia) and behind-the-meter generation (11-49 GW, Bloom Energy fuel cells) offer upside, but labor shortages (140K+ skilled trades needed by 2030) and political pushback limit how fast the gap closes.
